question: Oxygen makes up roughly 21% of the atmosphere by volume at every altitude. The reason hypoxia still develops as altitude increases is that:

options.text: The lungs become physically smaller at altitude, so each breath holds less air and the tissues receive less oxygen from each one that is taken in, whatever the pressure outside
The total (barometric) pressure falls with altitude, so the partial pressure of oxygen in each breath falls even though its percentage stays the same
The percentage of oxygen itself falls sharply above 10,000 ft
Nitrogen is absorbed by the lungs in place of oxygen at altitude

explanation: By Dalton's Law, the partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is its fraction of the total pressure. Oxygen's 21% share stays constant, but as total barometric pressure drops with altitude, the absolute partial pressure of oxygen drops with it — that falling partial pressure, not a changing percentage, is what starves the body of oxygen.

question: "Hypoxic hypoxia" specifically describes a shortage of oxygen at the tissues caused by:

options.text: A reduced number of red blood cells available to carry oxygen
Reduced blood flow to a particular limb, which is caused by the body restricting circulation to the extremities in cold conditions and so cannot be produced by altitude
A reduced partial pressure of oxygen in the air being breathed, as happens with increasing altitude
A chemical that prevents haemoglobin from releasing oxygen to the tissues

explanation: The four classic types of hypoxia are distinguished by cause: hypoxic (low inspired partial pressure, as at altitude), anaemic (reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood), stagnant (poor circulation) and histotoxic (tissues unable to use oxygen even when it is delivered, as with cyanide poisoning).

question: A particularly dangerous feature of hypoxic hypoxia, compared with many other physiological threats, is that:

options.text: It only ever develops after several hours at altitude
It affects muscles before it affects the brain, which is why a hypoxic person usually notices a loss of strength in the arms long before any change in their judgement or thinking
It impairs judgement before it is subjectively noticed, so the person affected often feels fine and may even feel euphoric while their performance is already degraded
It always produces severe pain, making it impossible to miss

explanation: Early hypoxia often brings a false sense of well-being along with impaired judgement, memory and coordination — the very faculties a person would need to recognise that something is wrong. That is why hypoxia is taught as a threat that must be anticipated rather than waited for.

question: The progression of hypoxic hypoxia with increasing altitude is usually described in a series of stages or zones. Which lists them in the correct order, from sea level upward?

options.text: Critical, disturbance, compensatory, indifferent, which reverses the usual order in which the body's responses to a falling oxygen supply are described in aviation training courses
Indifferent, compensatory, disturbance (or distress), critical
Critical, disturbance, compensatory, indifferent
Compensatory, critical, indifferent, disturbance

explanation: At low altitude the body shows essentially no effect (indifferent stage). As altitude rises the body first compensates (increased heart and breathing rate), then compensation becomes insufficient and performance visibly degrades (disturbance), and finally consciousness itself is lost (critical stage).

question: In the "compensatory stage" of hypoxia, the body's typical response is to:

options.text: Reduce heart rate to conserve energy, since the body slows its circulation as soon as the oxygen supply begins to fall so that less energy is spent on pumping the blood around
Reduce heart rate to conserve energy
Increase heart rate and breathing rate to try to deliver more oxygen to the tissues
Immediately lose consciousness

explanation: In the compensatory stage the cardiovascular and respiratory systems work harder — faster pulse, faster and deeper breathing — in an attempt to offset the lower oxygen partial pressure. This largely succeeds at moderate altitudes but becomes inadequate as altitude increases further.

question: Which factor would make an individual more susceptible to hypoxia at a given altitude, for the same oxygen supply?

options.text: Having a slower-than-normal metabolic rate
Being well rested and well hydrated
Being seated rather than standing, which raises the pressure within the lungs and so reduces the amount of oxygen that the blood is able to pick up in each breath taken
Having smoked recently, so that some haemoglobin is already carrying carbon monoxide instead of oxygen

explanation: Anything that already reduces the blood's effective oxygen-carrying capacity (recent smoking, anaemia, alcohol, illness, fatigue) effectively moves the onset of noticeable hypoxia to a lower altitude, because less reserve capacity is available to begin with.

question: Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) is defined as:

options.text: The time from the onset of a hypoxic exposure (such as a cabin depressurization) until a person is no longer able to take effective corrective action
The time it takes an aircraft to descend from cruise altitude to a safe altitude
A fixed time that is the same at every altitude, since the body's tolerance for low oxygen is set by its own design and is not affected by how high the aircraft happens to be flying
The total time a person can survive without oxygen before death

explanation: TUC is about usefulness, not survival: it is the window during which a hypoxic person can still recognise the problem and act on it — for example, donning an oxygen mask — before judgement and coordination are too impaired to do so.

question: As cabin altitude following a decompression increases from, say, 25,000 ft toward 40,000 ft, Time of Useful Consciousness:

options.text: Increases, because thinner air is easier for the lungs to process
Stays essentially constant regardless of altitude
Falls sharply, from a few minutes to a matter of seconds
Becomes infinite above 35,000 ft due to reduced air resistance

explanation: TUC shortens dramatically with altitude. At the lower end of this range there may be several minutes to act; well above it, TUC can fall to only a handful of seconds, which is exactly why crew oxygen must be donned immediately, not after assessing the situation.

question: Effective Performance Time (EPT) differs from Time of Useful Consciousness mainly in that EPT:

options.text: Is measured from the moment of a rapid decompression itself, so it also includes any time lost to the shock, cold and noise of the event, not just the hypoxic effect
Only applies to passengers, never to crew
Is always longer than TUC
Only applies to passengers, never to crew, because the crew are protected by their oxygen masks and so are always able to perform effectively throughout any decompression event

explanation: EPT accounts for the practical reality of a sudden decompression — the startle, noise, cold and possible injury — on top of the purely hypoxic effect that TUC measures, so EPT is generally the shorter, more conservative figure of the two.

question: Hyperventilation is best described as:

options.text: A deliberate technique used to treat hypoxia, since breathing faster than the body needs is the standard way to raise blood oxygen quickly in an emergency at altitude
A condition that only occurs at very high altitude
Breathing too slowly to meet the body's oxygen demand
Breathing faster or more deeply than the body's metabolic needs require, washing out carbon dioxide faster than it is produced

explanation: Hyperventilation is over-breathing relative to need, most often triggered by anxiety, stress or pain rather than by a genuine oxygen shortage. It drives down carbon dioxide levels in the blood faster than metabolism replaces them.

question: The characteristic symptoms of hyperventilation — tingling in the fingers and around the lips, light-headedness and a feeling of breathlessness despite rapid breathing — arise mainly because:

options.text: Carbon dioxide is actively toxic at any concentration
Blood oxygen levels rise to dangerously high levels
The heart stops beating temporarily, because the shortage of carbon dioxide slows the heart so much that the blood stops moving to the brain for a few seconds at a time
The resulting fall in blood carbon dioxide shifts blood chemistry toward alkalinity (respiratory alkalosis), which alters nerve and blood vessel function

explanation: It is the loss of carbon dioxide, not a lack of oxygen, that produces these symptoms. The resulting respiratory alkalosis constricts some blood vessels and alters nerve excitability, producing tingling, dizziness and the paradoxical sense of breathlessness.

question: Hypoxia and hyperventilation can present with overlapping symptoms (light-headedness, tingling, poor concentration), which matters because:

options.text: Hypoxia cannot occur below 25,000 ft, so the two are never confused in light aircraft
Hyperventilation only occurs on the ground, so altitude symptoms are always hypoxia, and a pilot who feels light-headed in the air can therefore safely ignore the symptom
The treatment for both is identical in every respect, so the distinction has no practical importance
Misdiagnosing hypoxia as simple anxiety-driven hyperventilation could delay the correct response of using supplemental oxygen

explanation: Because the two conditions can look alike, standard guidance is to treat ambiguous symptoms as hypoxia first — go onto oxygen or descend — since that is the more immediately dangerous possibility, and only then consider controlled, slower breathing if hyperventilation is confirmed.

question: A practical first step to help a passenger who is hyperventilating due to anxiety, once a medical cause has been ruled out, is to:

options.text: Encourage slower, controlled breathing and reassure them, which helps carbon dioxide levels return to normal
Ask them to hold their breath for as long as possible, which raises blood carbon dioxide and is a recognised way to relieve the feeling of breathlessness at altitude
Encourage them to breathe even faster to "get it over with"
Immediately put them on 100% supplemental oxygen regardless of cause

explanation: Since hyperventilation's symptoms come from excess carbon dioxide loss rather than too little oxygen, the useful response is to slow the breathing rate down — talking calmly or counting breaths — rather than adding oxygen, which does not address the actual imbalance.

question: A pressurized airliner cruising at 38,000 ft typically maintains a cabin altitude that is:

options.text: Identical to the aircraft's actual cruising altitude
Much lower than the actual cruising altitude, commonly in the general region of 6,000-8,000 ft
Always exactly sea level, because pressurisation brings the cabin back to ground pressure as soon as the aircraft reaches its cruising altitude and then holds it there
Higher than the aircraft's actual cruising altitude

explanation: Pressurization keeps the cabin at a far lower equivalent altitude than the aircraft actually flies at, typically in the region of several thousand feet, which keeps occupants comfortable without requiring the structure to withstand sea-level pressure at altitude.

question: The key difference between a "slow" (or gradual) cabin decompression and a "rapid" (or explosive) decompression is:

options.text: How quickly cabin pressure falls, which in turn determines how quickly symptoms and other physical effects develop and how much warning the crew gets
That a rapid decompression can only happen below 10,000 ft
That a slow decompression is always more dangerous, because the body adapts to a gradual fall in pressure and so suffers greater harm than from a sudden loss of cabin air
Only the final cabin altitude reached, not the rate of change

explanation: The rate of pressure loss, not just the final altitude, determines the danger. A slow leak may go unnoticed for a while and give time to react; a rapid or explosive decompression gives little or no warning and can itself cause injury from the pressure change and flying debris.

question: A sudden fogging or misting of the cabin air immediately after a rapid decompression is most directly explained by:

options.text: An optical illusion with no physical cause
Fuel vapour entering the cabin
Water vapour in the cabin air condensing as the air expands and cools suddenly
Smoke from an electrical fire, which always accompanies decompression

explanation: The rapid expansion of cabin air as pressure drops causes a sharp temperature drop, which can condense the water vapour normally present in cabin air into a visible mist — a physical, not hazardous, side effect of the pressure change itself.

question: Decompression sickness (DCS) is caused by:

options.text: Excess carbon dioxide accumulating in the joints
Bacterial infection triggered by low cabin humidity
A direct lack of oxygen reaching the brain
Nitrogen dissolved in body tissues coming out of solution as gas bubbles when ambient pressure falls too quickly

explanation: The body's tissues normally hold dissolved nitrogen in equilibrium with ambient pressure. If that pressure drops faster than the nitrogen can be safely off-gassed through the lungs, it can come out of solution as bubbles within tissue and blood, producing decompression sickness.

question: "The bends", the most commonly described symptom of decompression sickness, refers to:

options.text: A sharp pain in the chest caused only by cabin noise
Pain in and around the joints, caused by nitrogen bubbles forming in or near them
A skin rash with no internal cause
Difficulty speaking clearly

explanation: Joint and limb pain ("the bends") is the classic and most frequently reported form of DCS, though bubbles can also affect the skin ("the creeps"), the lungs ("the chokes") and, in more serious cases, the nervous system.

question: Why is scuba diving shortly before a flight considered a significant risk factor for decompression sickness, even in a normally pressurized cabin?

options.text: Diving loads the body's tissues with extra dissolved nitrogen, and climbing to even a modest cabin altitude afterward can be enough to let that nitrogen come out of solution
Diving has no bearing on DCS risk during a normal flight; the two are unrelated
DCS can only occur in the water, never after returning to the surface
Scuba equipment leaves residual compressed air in the lungs for days

explanation: A dive increases ambient pressure well above the surface value, loading tissues with extra dissolved nitrogen. Flying soon afterward adds a further pressure reduction on top of what surfacing already caused, which is why a surface interval before flying is standard safety guidance for divers.

question: Immediate first aid for a suspected case of decompression sickness, once on the ground, typically includes:

options.text: Giving 100% oxygen and arranging urgent medical evaluation, since more serious cases may require recompression treatment
Encouraging vigorous exercise to work the bubbles out of the joints
Waiting several days to see whether symptoms resolve on their own before seeking help
Immediately climbing to a higher cabin altitude

explanation: High-concentration oxygen helps wash out nitrogen and supports the tissues while definitive care is arranged. Severe or persistent DCS may need treatment in a recompression (hyperbaric) chamber, which is why prompt medical evaluation — not waiting it out — is the standard advice.

question: Regulatory requirements for supplemental oxygen use become progressively stricter as cruising altitude increases mainly because:

options.text: The rules are arbitrary and unrelated to physiology

The margin against hypoxia narrows as ambient partial pressure of oxygen falls, so the consequences of an unprotected exposure (loss of cabin pressure, mask failure) become more severe and arrive more quickly
Higher altitudes always have more oxygen available, so there is more to lose
Supplemental oxygen is only needed to prevent engine icing at altitude

explanation: As cruising altitude rises, both the cabin's normal equivalent altitude and the severity of a potential depressurization increase, shrinking the time available to react. Oxygen requirements are graduated to match that shrinking margin, not set arbitrarily.

question: Among the body's tissues, the retina is particularly sensitive to even mild hypoxia because:

options.text: The retina is unaffected by blood oxygen levels
The rod cells responsible for night vision have a very high oxygen demand relative to other parts of the eye
Hypoxia affects colour vision long before it affects night vision
The retina has no blood supply at all

explanation: Rod cells, which dominate low-light vision, have a high metabolic and oxygen demand. This is why night vision is often one of the earliest functions to degrade under mild hypoxia, well before more obvious symptoms appear — a key reason night flights at altitude call for early, generous use of oxygen.

question: A person who lives and works at high altitude for an extended period typically becomes partially acclimatised to it mainly because the body:

options.text: Permanently enlarges the lungs within days
Stops requiring any oxygen at all
Increases red blood cell production over time, raising the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity to partly offset the lower partial pressure
Reduces its oxygen demand to zero

explanation: Over days to weeks, sustained exposure to reduced oxygen partial pressure stimulates increased red blood cell production, which raises the blood's carrying capacity and partly compensates for the altitude — a slow, gradual adaptation, not an instant fix for a short flight.

question: Why is exposure to cold, as might follow a rapid decompression at high altitude, considered to worsen the effects of hypoxia rather than simply being a separate problem?

options.text: Cold only matters if the person is also hyperventilating
Cold has no physiological effect on a hypoxic person
Cold adds its own physiological stress and distraction on top of impaired judgement, compounding an already reduced capacity to respond effectively
Cold increases the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, so it actually helps

explanation: A rapid decompression at altitude brings sudden cold alongside falling oxygen partial pressure. The combined stress — shivering, pain, distraction — further degrades the attention and coordination that are already reduced by hypoxia, which is part of why EPT is shorter than TUC alone would suggest.
